newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Troops help calm Albania but can't stop exodus.
newsitem.headline: Troops help calm Albania but can't stop exodus.

text.p: International troops in Albania to oversee aid deliveries have helped calm the situation but can do little to stop the flood of Albanians fleeing the country, the head of a multi-national force said on Monday.
"The presence of the multi-national force is starting to achieve one of its aims which is to gain a secure environment," Lieutenant General Luciano Forlani told a news conference.

However the troops do not have the authority to stop the flood of Albanians attempting to flee since the collapse of high-risk savings funds swept the Balkan country into near anarchy earlier this year.
"This is not a police mission," said Forlani, leading the United Nations approved mission which has a three-month mandate.
At least 15,000 Albanians have fled across the Adriatic to Italy since February, with organised gangs running the traffic and charging $500 a head for a space on a boat.
Italian authorities on Monday sent home 180 Albanians, classified as "undesirables", who arrived at Bari in southern Italy on Sunday on a tanker packed with 1,229 Albanians.
The ageing vessel, the Irini, set sail late Saturday from Velipoje Beach, near Shkroder in northern Albania.
This was the second boat in a week to leave from Velipoje, an area free of international troops. Hundreds of other Albanians were still waiting there on Monday for another ship.

Ships carrying illegal immigrants have stopped running from the south of the country since some of the 6,300 soldiers of the multi-national force, which started arriving in Albania three weeks ago, secured the port of Vlore.
Forlani said Spanish soldiers stationed at Shengjin in northern Albania visited Velipoje on Monday, but only to ensure there was no threat to aid distribution.
"The Spanish contingent was just carrying out reconnaissance along the route," he said. "They were not doing anything more than this."
Security has become a major issue in Albania where guns are commonplace.

State arsenals were looted during the chaos in early March and unofficial estimates suggest up to one million guns are spread across the 3.4 million population, some in the hands of armed gangs roaming many parts of the country.
A Spanish soldier stationed at Shengjin on Monday paid $1 for 100 machine gun bullets and a few packets of explosives from a seven-year-old boy, Albanian news agency ATA said.
A spokesman for the Spanish troops said the soldier heard the child was in possession of the ammunition and wanted to avoid any danger to the boy's life.
"The child could have endangered his own life and that of the others," he said, adding the multi-national troops were not in Albania to buy or collect weapons.
